sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Solve the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x}{y}$, given that $y=3$ when $x=0$.
questions.answer: Separate: $y\,dy=x\,dx$. Integrate: $\frac{y^2}{2}=\frac{x^2}{2}+C$. Using $y=3,x=0$: $\frac{9}{2}=C$. So $y^2=x^2+9$, giving $y=\sqrt{x^2+9}$ (taking the positive root since $y=3>0$).
questions.explanation: Separate: $y\,dy=x\,dx$. Integrate: $\frac{y^2}{2}=\frac{x^2}{2}+C$. Using $y=3,x=0$: $\frac{9}{2}=C$. So $y^2=x^2+9$, giving $y=\sqrt{x^2+9}$ (taking the positive root since $y=3>0$).

questions.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy$, given that $y=5$ when $x=0$.
questions.answer: Separate: $\frac{dy}{y}=2x\,dx$. Integrate: $\ln|y|=x^2+C$. So $y=Ae^{x^2}$ for some constant $A$. Using $y=5,x=0$: $A=5$. Solution: $y=5e^{x^2}$.
questions.explanation: Separate: $\frac{dy}{y}=2x\,dx$. Integrate: $\ln|y|=x^2+C$. So $y=Ae^{x^2}$ for some constant $A$. Using $y=5,x=0$: $A=5$. Solution: $y=5e^{x^2}$.

questions.q: A population $P$ grows at a rate proportional to its current size, modeled by $\frac{dP}{dt}=kP$. If the population doubles every 5 years, find $k$, to three decimal places.
questions.answer: Solving the DE: $P(t)=P_0e^{kt}$. Doubling: $2P_0=P_0e^{5k}$, so $e^{5k}=2$, giving $5k=\ln2$, $k=\frac{\ln2}{5}\approx0.139$.
questions.explanation: Solving the DE: $P(t)=P_0e^{kt}$. Doubling: $2P_0=P_0e^{5k}$, so $e^{5k}=2$, giving $5k=\ln2$, $k=\frac{\ln2}{5}\approx0.139$.

questions.q: Newton's law of cooling states $\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_a)$, where $T_a$ is ambient temperature. Solve this differential equation for $T(t)$ in terms of the initial temperature $T_0$.
questions.answer: Separate: $\frac{dT}{T-T_a}=-k\,dt$. Integrate: $\ln|T-T_a|=-kt+C$. So $T-T_a=Ae^{-kt}$. At $t=0$, $T=T_0$, so $A=T_0-T_a$. Solution: $T(t)=T_a+(T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}$.
questions.explanation: Separate: $\frac{dT}{T-T_a}=-k\,dt$. Integrate: $\ln|T-T_a|=-kt+C$. So $T-T_a=Ae^{-kt}$. At $t=0$, $T=T_0$, so $A=T_0-T_a$. Solution: $T(t)=T_a+(T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}$.

questions.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=6$ using an integrating factor, given $y=1$ when $x=0$.
questions.answer: Integrating factor: $e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x}$. Multiply through: $e^{2x}\frac{dy}{dx}+2e^{2x}y=6e^{2x}$, i.e. $\frac{d}{dx}(ye^{2x})=6e^{2x}$. Integrate: $ye^{2x}=3e^{2x}+C$, so $y=3+Ce^{-2x}$. Using $y=1,x=0$: $1=3+C$, so $C=-2$. Solution: $y=3-2e^{-2x}$.
questions.explanation: Integrating factor: $e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x}$. Multiply through: $e^{2x}\frac{dy}{dx}+2e^{2x}y=6e^{2x}$, i.e. $\frac{d}{dx}(ye^{2x})=6e^{2x}$. Integrate: $ye^{2x}=3e^{2x}+C$, so $y=3+Ce^{-2x}$. Using $y=1,x=0$: $1=3+C$, so $C=-2$. Solution: $y=3-2e^{-2x}$.

The differential equation $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\omega^2x$ describes simple harmonic motion. Verify that $x(t)=A\cos(\omega t)$ is a solution.
questions.answer: $\frac{dx}{dt}=-A\omega\sin(\omega t)$. $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-A\omega^2\cos(\omega t)=-\omega^2\left(A\cos(\omega t)\right)=-\omega^2x$, confirming $x(t)=A\cos(\omega t)$ satisfies the differential equation.
questions.explanation: $\frac{dx}{dt}=-A\omega\sin(\omega t)$. $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-A\omega^2\cos(\omega t)=-\omega^2\left(A\cos(\omega t)\right)=-\omega^2x$, confirming $x(t)=A\cos(\omega t)$ satisfies the differential equation.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Find the general solution of $\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2$, and explain what the arbitrary constant represents geometrically.
questions.target: Family of solution curves and particular solutions
questions.answer: Integrating directly: $y=x^3+C$. The constant $C$ represents a vertical shift — the general solution is a whole family of curves, all with the same shape (since they share the same derivative $3x^2$ at every $x$), just shifted up or down by different amounts.
questions.explanation: Integrating directly: $y=x^3+C$. The constant $C$ represents a vertical shift — the general solution is a whole family of curves, all with the same shape (since they share the same derivative $3x^2$ at every $x$), just shifted up or down by different amounts.

questions.q: A tank drains such that $\frac{dV}{dt}=-k\sqrt{V}$ for some constant $k>0$, where $V$ is the volume of water. Solve this differential equation for $V(t)$, given $V(0)=V_0$.
questions.target: Family of solution curves and particular solutions
questions.answer: Separate: $\frac{dV}{\sqrt{V}}=-k\,dt$, i.e. $V^{-1/2}\,dV=-k\,dt$. Integrate: $2\sqrt{V}=-kt+C$. Using $V(0)=V_0$: $2\sqrt{V_0}=C$. So $2\sqrt{V}=-kt+2\sqrt{V_0}$, giving $\sqrt{V}=\sqrt{V_0}-\frac{kt}{2}$, so $V(t)=\left(\sqrt{V_0}-\frac{kt}{2}\right)^2$.
questions.explanation: Separate: $\frac{dV}{\sqrt{V}}=-k\,dt$, i.e. $V^{-1/2}\,dV=-k\,dt$. Integrate: $2\sqrt{V}=-kt+C$. Using $V(0)=V_0$: $2\sqrt{V_0}=C$. So $2\sqrt{V}=-kt+2\sqrt{V_0}$, giving $\sqrt{V}=\sqrt{V_0}-\frac{kt}{2}$, so $V(t)=\left(\sqrt{V_0}-\frac{kt}{2}\right)^2$.

questions.q: Verify that $y=e^{2x}$ is a solution of the differential equation $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-5\frac{dy}{dx}+6y=0$.
questions.target: Verifying a solution to a second-order differential equation
questions.answer: $\frac{dy}{dx}=2e^{2x}$. $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4e^{2x}$. Substituting: $4e^{2x}-5(2e^{2x})+6e^{2x}=4e^{2x}-10e^{2x}+6e^{2x}=0e^{2x}=0$, confirming $y=e^{2x}$ is a solution.
questions.explanation: $\frac{dy}{dx}=2e^{2x}$. $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4e^{2x}$. Substituting: $4e^{2x}-5(2e^{2x})+6e^{2x}=4e^{2x}-10e^{2x}+6e^{2x}=0e^{2x}=0$, confirming $y=e^{2x}$ is a solution.

questions.q: A differential equation is given by $\frac{dy}{dx}=x-y$. Find the gradient of the solution curve at the points $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, and $(1,1)$, and explain what a slope field represents.
questions.answer: At $(0,0)$: gradient $=0-0=0$. At $(1,0)$: gradient $=1-0=1$. At $(1,1)$: gradient $=1-1=0$. A slope field is a diagram that plots a short line segment of the correct gradient at many points in the plane, without solving the equation explicitly — sketching a solution curve then amounts to drawing a curve that follows the direction of the segments at every point it passes through.
questions.explanation: At $(0,0)$: gradient $=0-0=0$. At $(1,0)$: gradient $=1-0=1$. At $(1,1)$: gradient $=1-1=0$. A slope field is a diagram that plots a short line segment of the correct gradient at many points in the plane, without solving the equation explicitly — sketching a solution curve then amounts to drawing a curve that follows the direction of the segments at every point it passes through.

questions.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y}{x}=x$ for $x>0$ using an integrating factor, given $y=2$ when $x=1$.
questions.target: Solving a linear differential equation with an initial condition
questions.answer: Rewrite in standard form: $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x}y=x$. Integrating factor: $e^{\int-\frac{1}{x}dx}=e^{-\ln x}=\frac{1}{x}$. Multiply through: $\frac{1}{x}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x^2}y=1$, i.e. $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)=1$. Integrate: $\frac{y}{x}=x+C$, so $y=x^2+Cx$. Using $y=2,x=1$: $2=1+C$, so $C=1$. Solution: $y=x^2+x$.
questions.explanation: Rewrite in standard form: $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x}y=x$. Integrating factor: $e^{\int-\frac{1}{x}dx}=e^{-\ln x}=\frac{1}{x}$. Multiply through: $\frac{1}{x}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x^2}y=1$, i.e. $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)=1$. Integrate: $\frac{y}{x}=x+C$, so $y=x^2+Cx$. Using $y=2,x=1$: $2=1+C$, so $C=1$. Solution: $y=x^2+x$.

questions.q: A population $P$ grows according to the logistic differential equation $\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(10-P)$. Using the partial fraction decomposition $\frac{1}{P(10-P)}=\frac{1}{10P}+\frac{1}{10(10-P)}$, solve for $P$ in terms of $t$, given $P(0)=1$ and leaving $k$ as an unknown constant.
questions.answer: Separate: $\frac{dP}{P(10-P)}=k\,dt$. Integrate the left side using the given decomposition: $\frac{1}{10}\ln|P|-\frac{1}{10}\ln|10-P|=kt+C$, i.e. $\frac{1}{10}\ln\left|\frac{P}{10-P}\right|=kt+C$. Using $P(0)=1$: $\frac{1}{10}\ln\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)=C$. So $\ln\left|\frac{P}{10-P}\right|=10kt+\ln\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)$, giving $\frac{P}{10-P}=\frac{1}{9}e^{10kt}$. Solving for $P$: $9P=(10-P)e^{10kt}$, so $P(9+e^{10kt})=10e^{10kt}$, giving $P=\frac{10e^{10kt}}{9+e^{10kt}}$.
questions.explanation: Separate: $\frac{dP}{P(10-P)}=k\,dt$. Integrate the left side using the given decomposition: $\frac{1}{10}\ln|P|-\frac{1}{10}\ln|10-P|=kt+C$, i.e. $\frac{1}{10}\ln\left|\frac{P}{10-P}\right|=kt+C$. Using $P(0)=1$: $\frac{1}{10}\ln\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)=C$. So $\ln\left|\frac{P}{10-P}\right|=10kt+\ln\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)$, giving $\frac{P}{10-P}=\frac{1}{9}e^{10kt}$. Solving for $P$: $9P=(10-P)e^{10kt}$, so $P(9+e^{10kt})=10e^{10kt}$, giving $P=\frac{10e^{10kt}}{9+e^{10kt}}$.

questions.q: State the order of each of the following differential equations: (a) $\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-2y$, (b) $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}+4\frac{dy}{dx}-y=0$, (c) $\frac{d^3y}{dx^3}=\sin x$.
questions.target: Checking the order and degree of a differential equation
questions.answer: The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative present. (a) Only a first derivative appears, so this is a first-order differential equation. (b) The highest derivative is $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, so this is second-order. (c) The highest derivative is $\frac{d^3y}{dx^3}$, so this is third-order.
questions.explanation: The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative present. (a) Only a first derivative appears, so this is a first-order differential equation. (b) The highest derivative is $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, so this is second-order. (c) The highest derivative is $\frac{d^3y}{dx^3}$, so this is third-order.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.25$ to estimate $y(0.5)$ for $\frac{dy}{dx}=2x$, given $y(0)=1$, showing each step, and compare with the exact solution $y=x^2+1$.
questions.target: Using Euler's method with a smaller step size
questions.answer: Euler's method: $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\cdot f(x_n,y_n)$. Step 1 ($x_0=0,y_0=1$): $y_1=1+0.25(2\cdot0)=1+0=1$. Step 2 ($x_1=0.25,y_1=1$): $y_2=1+0.25(2\cdot0.25)=1+0.125=1.125$. Estimate: $y(0.5)\approx1.125$. Exact solution: $y(0.5)=(0.5)^2+1=1.25$. The Euler estimate underestimates the true value, since the method uses the derivative only at the start of each interval rather than accounting for how the derivative changes within it.
questions.explanation: Euler's method: $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\cdot f(x_n,y_n)$. Step 1 ($x_0=0,y_0=1$): $y_1=1+0.25(2\cdot0)=1+0=1$. Step 2 ($x_1=0.25,y_1=1$): $y_2=1+0.25(2\cdot0.25)=1+0.125=1.125$. Estimate: $y(0.5)\approx1.125$. Exact solution: $y(0.5)=(0.5)^2+1=1.25$. The Euler estimate underestimates the true value, since the method uses the derivative only at the start of each interval rather than accounting for how the derivative changes within it.

questions.q: Solve the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}$ for $x>0$, given $y=6$ when $x=2$, and describe the family of curves this represents.
questions.target: Using Euler's method with a smaller step size
questions.answer: Separate: $\frac{dy}{y}=\frac{dx}{x}$. Integrate: $\ln|y|=\ln|x|+C$, so $y=Ax$ for some constant $A$. Using $y=6,x=2$: $6=2A$, so $A=3$. Solution: $y=3x$. This represents the family of straight lines through the origin; the particular solution satisfying the initial condition is the specific line with slope $3$.
questions.explanation: Separate: $\frac{dy}{y}=\frac{dx}{x}$. Integrate: $\ln|y|=\ln|x|+C$, so $y=Ax$ for some constant $A$. Using $y=6,x=2$: $6=2A$, so $A=3$. Solution: $y=3x$. This represents the family of straight lines through the origin; the particular solution satisfying the initial condition is the specific line with slope $3$.

questions.q: A cup of coffee at $90^\circ$C is placed in a room at ambient temperature $20^\circ$C. Using Newton's law of cooling, $T(t)=T_a+(T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}$, and given that after $10$ minutes the coffee has cooled to $60^\circ$C, find the value of $k$ to three decimal places.
questions.target: Using Euler's method with a smaller step size
questions.answer: Using $T_a=20$, $T_0=90$, and $T(10)=60$: $60=20+(90-20)e^{-10k}$, so $40=70e^{-10k}$, giving $e^{-10k}=\frac{4}{7}$. Taking natural logs: $-10k=\ln\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)\approx-0.5596$, so $k\approx0.056$.
questions.explanation: Using $T_a=20$, $T_0=90$, and $T(10)=60$: $60=20+(90-20)e^{-10k}$, so $40=70e^{-10k}$, giving $e^{-10k}=\frac{4}{7}$. Taking natural logs: $-10k=\ln\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)\approx-0.5596$, so $k\approx0.056$.

questions.q: This question has three parts. A tank initially contains $200$ litres of pure water. Salt water containing $3$ grams of salt per litre flows in at a rate of $2$ litres per minute, and the well-mixed solution flows out at the same rate, so the volume stays constant at $200$ litres. Let $S(t)$ be the amount of salt (in grams) in the tank at time $t$ minutes. (a) Explain why $\frac{dS}{dt}=6-\frac{S}{100}$. (b) Solve this differential equation for $S(t)$, given $S(0)=0$. (c) Find the amount of salt in the tank after $50$ minutes, to the nearest gram.
questions.target: Using Euler's method with a smaller step size
questions.answer: (a) Salt flows in at a rate of $3$ grams/litre $\times2$ litres/minute $=6$ grams/minute. Salt flows out at a rate proportional to the current concentration $\frac{S}{200}$ grams/litre, times the outflow rate of $2$ litres/minute, giving $\frac{2S}{200}=\frac{S}{100}$ grams/minute out. Net rate: $\frac{dS}{dt}=6-\frac{S}{100}$. (b) This is a linear first-order DE. Integrating factor: $e^{\int\frac{1}{100}dt}=e^{t/100}$. $\frac{d}{dt}\left(Se^{t/100}\right)=6e^{t/100}$. Integrating: $Se^{t/100}=600e^{t/100}+C$, so $S=600+Ce^{-t/100}$. Using $S(0)=0$: $0=600+C$, so $C=-600$. Solution: $S(t)=600\left(1-e^{-t/100}\right)$. (c) At $t=50$: $S(50)=600\left(1-e^{-0.5}\right)=600(1-0.6065)=600(0.3935)\approx236$ grams.
questions.explanation: (a) Salt flows in at a rate of $3$ grams/litre $\times2$ litres/minute $=6$ grams/minute. Salt flows out at a rate proportional to the current concentration $\frac{S}{200}$ grams/litre, times the outflow rate of $2$ litres/minute, giving $\frac{2S}{200}=\frac{S}{100}$ grams/minute out. Net rate: $\frac{dS}{dt}=6-\frac{S}{100}$. (b) This is a linear first-order DE. Integrating factor: $e^{\int\frac{1}{100}dt}=e^{t/100}$. $\frac{d}{dt}\left(Se^{t/100}\right)=6e^{t/100}$. Integrating: $Se^{t/100}=600e^{t/100}+C$, so $S=600+Ce^{-t/100}$. Using $S(0)=0$: $0=600+C$, so $C=-600$. Solution: $S(t)=600\left(1-e^{-t/100}\right)$. (c) At $t=50$: $S(50)=600\left(1-e^{-0.5}\right)=600(1-0.6065)=600(0.3935)\approx236$ grams.

questions.q: A cubic equation with real coefficients $x^{3} + 7x^{2} + 15x + 25 = 0$ has $-1 + 2i$ as one root. Find the real root.
questions.cross_lesson: 5.04 Graphs of Inverse Trigonometric Functions & Their Derivatives (AA HL)
questions.answer: Final Answer: -5. $\mathrm{Complex\ roots\ occur\ in\ conjugate\ pairs,\ so\ }-1 - 2i\mathrm{\ is\ also\ a\ root.\ Product\ of\ all\ three\ roots}=-d=-25\mathrm{,\ and\ }(-1 + 2i)(-1 - 2i)=5\mathrm{,\ so\ the\ real\ root}=\frac{-25}{5}=-5.$
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{Complex\ roots\ occur\ in\ conjugate\ pairs,\ so\ }-1 - 2i\mathrm{\ is\ also\ a\ root.\ Product\ of\ all\ three\ roots}=-d=-25\mathrm{,\ and\ }(-1 + 2i)(-1 - 2i)=5\mathrm{,\ so\ the\ real\ root}=\frac{-25}{5}=-5.$

questions.q: A cubic equation with real coefficients $x^{3} - 10x^{2} + 37x - 52 = 0$ has $3 + 2i$ as one root. Find the real root.
questions.answer: Final Answer: 4. $\mathrm{Complex\ roots\ occur\ in\ conjugate\ pairs,\ so\ }3 - 2i\mathrm{\ is\ also\ a\ root.\ Product\ of\ all\ three\ roots}=-d=52\mathrm{,\ and\ }(3 + 2i)(3 - 2i)=13\mathrm{,\ so\ the\ real\ root}=\frac{52}{13}=4.$
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{Complex\ roots\ occur\ in\ conjugate\ pairs,\ so\ }3 - 2i\mathrm{\ is\ also\ a\ root.\ Product\ of\ all\ three\ roots}=-d=52\mathrm{,\ and\ }(3 + 2i)(3 - 2i)=13\mathrm{,\ so\ the\ real\ root}=\frac{52}{13}=4.$

sections.heading: Part IV — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Foundational Concept Mastery (21–28)

questions.q: Solve the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2x}{y}$ with initial condition $y(0) = 4$ for $y > 0$.
questions.answer: Separate variables: $y dy = 2x dx$. Integrate: $\frac{1}{2}y^2 = x^2 + C \Rightarrow y^2 = 2x^2 + 2C$. Since $y(0) = 4$, $16 = 2C$. Thus $y^2 = 2x^2 + 16 \Rightarrow y = \sqrt{2x^2 + 16}$.
questions.explanation: Separate variables: $y dy = 2x dx$. Integrate: $\frac{1}{2}y^2 = x^2 + C \Rightarrow y^2 = 2x^2 + 2C$. Since $y(0) = 4$, $16 = 2C$. Thus $y^2 = 2x^2 + 16 \Rightarrow y = \sqrt{2x^2 + 16}$.

questions.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = -3y$ with $y(0) = 50$.
questions.answer: $\frac{1}{y} dy = -3 dx \Rightarrow \ln|y| = -3x + C \Rightarrow y = A e^{-3x}$. With $y(0) = 50$, $y = 50 e^{-3x}$.
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{y} dy = -3 dx \Rightarrow \ln|y| = -3x + C \Rightarrow y = A e^{-3x}$. With $y(0) = 50$, $y = 50 e^{-3x}$.

questions.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = (1 + y^2) e^x$ with $y(0) = 0$.
questions.answer: $\frac{1}{1 + y^2} dy = e^x dx \Rightarrow \arctan y = e^x + C$. With $y(0) = 0$, $\arctan 0 = e^0 + C \Rightarrow 0 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = -1$. Thus $\arctan y = e^x - 1 \Rightarrow y = \tan(e^x - 1)$.
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{1 + y^2} dy = e^x dx \Rightarrow \arctan y = e^x + C$. With $y(0) = 0$, $\arctan 0 = e^0 + C \Rightarrow 0 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = -1$. Thus $\arctan y = e^x - 1 \Rightarrow y = \tan(e^x - 1)$.

questions.q: For the linear differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$, what is the integrating factor $I(x)$?
questions.target: Integrating Factor Method for First-Order Linear ODEs
questions.answer: Multiplying by $I(x) = e^{\int P(x)dx}$ collapses the left-hand side into the product rule derivative $\frac{d}{dx}[I(x) y]$.
questions.explanation: Multiplying by $I(x) = e^{\int P(x)dx}$ collapses the left-hand side into the product rule derivative $\frac{d}{dx}[I(x) y]$.

questions.q: Find the integrating factor for $\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{3}{x}y = x^2$ for $x > 0$.
questions.target: Integrating Factor Method for First-Order Linear ODEs

questions.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} + 2y = 4$ with $y(0) = 5$.
questions.target: Integrating Factor Method for First-Order Linear ODEs
questions.answer: $I(x) = e^{2x}$. Multiplying: $\frac{d}{dx}[e^{2x} y] = 4e^{2x} \Rightarrow e^{2x}y = 2e^{2x} + C \Rightarrow y = 2 + C e^{-2x}$. Using $y(0) = 5 \Rightarrow 5 = 2 + C \Rightarrow C = 3$. Thus $y = 2 + 3e^{-2x}$.
questions.explanation: $I(x) = e^{2x}$. Multiplying: $\frac{d}{dx}[e^{2x} y] = 4e^{2x} \Rightarrow e^{2x}y = 2e^{2x} + C \Rightarrow y = 2 + C e^{-2x}$. Using $y(0) = 5 \Rightarrow 5 = 2 + C \Rightarrow C = 3$. Thus $y = 2 + 3e^{-2x}$.

questions.q: Which substitution transforms a homogeneous differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = f(y/x)$ into a separable equation?
questions.answer: Let $v = y/x \Rightarrow y = v x$. By the product rule, $\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$, reducing the ODE to $v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = f(v)$.
questions.explanation: Let $v = y/x \Rightarrow y = v x$. By the product rule, $\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$, reducing the ODE to $v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = f(v)$.

questions.q: Classify the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{2xy}$.
questions.answer: Dividing numerator and denominator by $x^2$ gives $\frac{1 + (y/x)^2}{2(y/x)}$, which is a function purely of $y/x$, classifying it as homogeneous.
questions.explanation: Dividing numerator and denominator by $x^2$ gives $\frac{1 + (y/x)^2}{2(y/x)}$, which is a function purely of $y/x$, classifying it as homogeneous.

questions.q: Using $y = vx$, what does $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x} + 1$ become?
questions.answer: Substitute $\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$ and $y/x = v$: $v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v + 1 \Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx} = 1$.
questions.explanation: Substitute $\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$ and $y/x = v$: $v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v + 1 \Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx} = 1$.

questions.q: What is Euler's recurrence relation for approximating solutions to $\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)$ with step size $h$?
questions.answer: Euler's method uses the tangent line approximation: $y_{n+1} = y_n + h \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(x_n, y_n)} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n)$.
questions.explanation: Euler's method uses the tangent line approximation: $y_{n+1} = y_n + h \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(x_n, y_n)} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n)$.

questions.q: Given $\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y$ with $y(0) = 1$, use Euler's method with step size $h = 0.1$ to find $y_1$ at $x = 0.1$.
Using the result above ($x_1 = 0.1, y_1 = 1.10$), find $y_2$ at $x = 0.2$ with $h = 0.1$.
A cubic equation with real coefficients $x^{3} + 6x^{2} + 10x + 8 = 0$ has $-1 + i$ as one root. Find the real root.
questions.answer: $\mathrm{Complex\ roots\ occur\ in\ conjugate\ pairs,\ so\ }-1 - i\mathrm{\ is\ also\ a\ root.\ Product\ of\ all\ three\ roots}=-d=-8\mathrm{,\ and\ }(-1 + i)(-1 - i)=2\mathrm{,\ so\ the\ real\ root}=\frac{-8}{2}=-4.$
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{Complex\ roots\ occur\ in\ conjugate\ pairs,\ so\ }-1 - i\mathrm{\ is\ also\ a\ root.\ Product\ of\ all\ three\ roots}=-d=-8\mathrm{,\ and\ }(-1 + i)(-1 - i)=2\mathrm{,\ so\ the\ real\ root}=\frac{-8}{2}=-4.$

questions.q: A cubic equation with real coefficients $x^{3} - 8x^{2} + 22x - 20 = 0$ has $3 + i$ as one root. Find the real root.

questions.answer: $\mathrm{Complex\ roots\ occur\ in\ conjugate\ pairs,\ so\ }3 - i\mathrm{\ is\ also\ a\ root.\ Product\ of\ all\ three\ roots}=-d=20\mathrm{,\ and\ }(3 + i)(3 - i)=10\mathrm{,\ so\ the\ real\ root}=\frac{20}{10}=2.$

questions.q: A graph has edges $1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-1$. Does it have an Euler circuit, an Euler trail (not circuit), or neither?
choices: $\mathrm{Euler\ trail\ exists,\ but\ not\ an\ Euler\ circuit}$
$\mathrm{Cannot\ be\ determined\ from\ the\ given\ information}$
$\mathrm{Neither\ an\ Euler\ trail\ nor\ circuit\ exists}$
questions.answer: $\mathrm{A\ connected\ graph\ has\ an\ Euler\ circuit\ iff\ every\ vertex\ has\ even\ degree;\ an\ Euler\ trail\ (not\ circuit)\ iff\ exactly\ 2\ vertices\ have\ odd\ degree.}$
